analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary national long-term care insurance program with payroll-deducted premiums and daily cash benefits for home-based care.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2009 with 27 cosponsors, the bill was referred to four House committees, never received a markup or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a national, voluntary disability insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services. Every worker would be automatically enrolled through their employer (with the right to opt out) and pay premiums by payroll deduction — $30 a month for people enrolling in the program's first year, less for low-income workers. Workers who later cannot perform basic daily activities like bathing or dressing would receive a cash benefit — $50 a day, or $100 a day for the most impaired — with no lifetime limit, to pay for home care aides, home modifications, transportation, respite care, and similar nonmedical help, including paying a family caregiver. It also adds a tax deduction for premiums, a tax credit for low-income enrollees, and a tax credit for employers that withhold the premiums.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families who eventually need long-term care — a cost that most private insurance does not cover and that Medicaid only pays after a family has spent down its savings. People with preexisting conditions could enroll, since the bill bars any underwriting. Low-income enrollees (under 150% of poverty) would pay only nominal premiums and get a 50% tax credit below 250% of poverty. Family caregivers could be paid out of the cash benefit, and states would see some of their Medicaid home-care costs offset.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and families facing long-term care

how_it_helps.text: Creates a cash benefit of $50 per day (tier I) or $100 per day (tier II) for enrollees who can no longer perform basic daily activities, with no lifetime cap, usable for home care aides, home modifications, accessible transportation, homemaker services, respite care, and personal assistance.
Bars any underwriting: no one can be charged more or excluded based on health, and premiums are the same for everyone enrolling in the program's first year regardless of age.

Provides nominal premiums for workers with income under 150% of the poverty line, a refundable tax credit covering 50% of premiums for enrollees under 250% of poverty, an above-the-line deduction for other enrollees, and a tax credit for employers that withhold premiums.

Expressly allows benefits to be used to pay family caregivers and requires states to designate or create entities to serve as employers and fiscal agents for personal care attendant workers, including in rural areas.

Requires benefit applications to be decided within 30 days (approved automatically after 45), guarantees an appeal, and disregards the benefit when determining eligibility for Medicaid, Social Security, food stamps, and other programs.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, through an automatic monthly payroll deduction they must actively opt out of — $30 a month in the program's first year, rising for later enrollees. The federal Treasury would appropriate additional sums in fiscal years 2013 through 2017 to keep the fund solvent while the first cohorts of beneficiaries emerge. Private long-term care insurers would face a public competitor that accepts applicants regardless of health.

drawbacks.text: Enrollment is voluntary with an opt-out and there is no underwriting, so people who expect to need care have the strongest reason to stay in while healthy workers have the strongest reason to leave — the classic adverse-selection problem in insurance, which tends to push premiums up or force benefit cuts over time. The bill itself anticipates this, directing the Secretary to recalculate premiums from 2017 if more than 40% of the fund would be needed for benefits, while capping any increase at 50% or twice the original premium.

The $30 flat first-year premium applies regardless of the enrollee's age, and premiums are capped rather than guaranteed to cover costs, so the program's solvency depends on projections the bill itself flags as uncertain.
The benefit is modest: $50–$100 a day covers in-home help and family caregiving but falls well short of the cost of a nursing home, and it pays for nonmedical supports only, not medical care.

Because workers are enrolled automatically and must opt out, some employees would end up paying premiums they did not actively choose, and employers take on a new withholding duty (softened by a 25% tax credit for their enrollment costs).

The bill appropriates unspecified federal general revenue for fiscal 2013–2017 to keep the fund solvent during its early years, an off-budget, lock-box-protected fund that federal budget rules would treat separately from the deficit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: most working families are one long-term-care event away from draining savings, because neither private insurance (heavily underwritten and expensive) nor Medicaid (available only after spending down) fills it well. No underwriting and paid family caregiving would genuinely help people private insurers turn away. But the design carries a serious known flaw — a voluntary program with no underwriting tends to attract those who most expect to need care, threatening solvency — and the benefit is modest relative to nursing-home costs. Congress never tested the idea in this bill, and when a version of the CLASS Act was later enacted inside the Affordable Care Act, federal actuaries concluded its premiums could not sustain it, and it was repealed. The need was real; the design of this particular program was not clearly workable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and to a Health subcommittee the next day; it never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on March 25, 2009, joined by Reps. John Dingell and Patrick Kennedy, and it was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Rules, and Budget Committees.
On March 26, 2009, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce; no further action of any kind is recorded for the rest of the Congress.
The bill drew 27 cosponsors — 26 House Democrats and 1 House Republican.
No committee reported the bill, no vote occurred in either chamber, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private long-term care insurers never faced the no-underwriting public competitor this bill would have created. Families continued to face long-term care costs with only private policies or spend-down-to-Medicaid as options. A version of the CLASS Act was enacted as part of the Affordable Care Act in 2010, but it was later repealed after federal actuaries concluded its premiums could not cover its costs.

sides.party_line_note: 26 of the bill's 27 cosponsors were House Democrats and only 1 was a Republican; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would have created a public program that accepts applicants of any health at a flat premium, undercutting private policies that charge steep rates or deny coverage to people with preexisting conditions. The industry's interest in this bill ran against the families it prices out.

industries.industry: Home care and personal-assistance providers and care workers
industries.note: Cash benefits flow directly to home care aides, home modifications, respite care, and paid family caregivers, and the bill requires states to build an infrastructure of employers and fiscal agents for personal care attendant workers, including in rural areas.
CLASS benefits would partially offset state costs for home and community-based care and, long term, could reduce the number of people forced to spend down into Medicaid for long-term care.
Employers would take on a duty to automatically enroll workers and withhold premiums, but would receive a 25% tax credit for those costs.
